q: Sandier soils on the western edge of the Bourgueil zone give lighter, earlier-drinking Cabernet Franc under a name of its own. Which?
exp: It is a separate appellation covering a single commune, generally more perfumed and quicker to open than Bourgueil itself. In practice the styles overlap heavily from producer to producer.

q: A light-bodied red arrives with raspberry, violet, pencil shavings and a green-pepper edge, on fine tannin and high acidity. Which grape and origin?
exp: The herbaceous note comes from pyrazines that ripeness reduces but never quite erases this far north. It is a signature rather than a fault, and it is why these wines take a light chill so well.

q: A dark, plummy Touraine red is labelled with the old French name for the variety Argentina calls Malbec. What is that name?
exp: Cot is the old French name for the variety Cahors calls Auxerrois and Argentina calls Malbec. In Touraine it makes a deeper, more brambly red than Cabernet Franc, often blended with it.

q: Chalky marl full of fossil oyster shells underlies the western slopes above Chavignol, the same seam that surfaces a hundred kilometres away in Chablis. What is it?
exp: Terres blanches is the local name across the western communes of Sancerre: heavy, water-retaining clay-limestone that ripens slowly and gives the broadest, most structured wines of the appellation. Caillottes, the stonier Portlandian limestone, gives quicker and more aromatic wine.

q: Growers on the eastern edge of the Centre, nearest the river, work stony ground of flint, and their wines are traditionally described as smoky. What is that soil called?
exp: Silex is flint, concentrated around Saint-Andelain and giving Pouilly-Fume its most celebrated wines, though Kimmeridgian marl covers more of the appellation. Whether the gunflint aroma really comes from the rock is disputed, but the wines from it are undeniably taut.

q: Red and rose Sancerre exist alongside the white. Which single variety fills them?
exp: Burgundy is close, and Pinot Noir was widely planted here before phylloxera. The reds are pale and red-fruited, and warmer recent vintages have made them considerably more serious.

q: One appellation in the village of Pouilly is reserved for Chasselas rather than Sauvignon Blanc. What is it called?
exp: Two appellations share one village and the difference is the grape. Chasselas is a neutral table grape and the wine is a curiosity, made in dwindling quantities.

q: Which older name for Sauvignon Blanc still appears on labels from Pouilly?
exp: Blanc Fume de Pouilly is the full traditional form, and the fume in the appellation name comes from it. California's Fume Blanc borrowed the word outright in the 1960s.

q: Barely twenty kilometres west of Sancerre, a smaller appellation grows Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir on the same Kimmeridgian marl. Which?
exp: Same soils, same grapes and the same styles in white, red and rose, with a fraction of the recognition. It is the standard recommendation when a guest wants Sancerre and balks at the price.

q: On sand and gravel terraces above the river Cher, one appellation of the Centre bottles white wine and nothing else. Which?
exp: White only, from Sauvignon Blanc, and one of the earliest appellations granted in France. The sandy soils warm early, so the wines tend to be riper and rounder than Sancerre.

q: Which appellation of the Centre is best known for a pale, delicate rose made from Pinot Gris?
exp: Pinot Gris for rose is unusual anywhere in France and is Reuilly's signature. The same appellation also makes Sauvignon Blanc whites and Pinot Noir reds.

q: A fresh goat cheese from a hamlet in the Sancerre hills is the textbook partner for the local white. Which cheese?
exp: The cheese and the wine come from the same slopes, and acidity is what makes the pairing work: it cuts the chalky richness of the curd rather than fighting it. The other three are Loire goat cheeses from further west.

q: Steep slopes directly above the water are favoured throughout the middle Loire. What does the river do for those vineyards?
opts: It cools the site enough to delay the harvest by a month
It moderates temperature and reflects light onto the slope
It supplies irrigation water permitted under the appellation rules
It raises humidity enough to prevent fungal disease altogether
exp: A large body of water warms slowly and cools slowly, softening both frost and heat spikes, and the reflected light eases ripening in a marginal climate. The same humidity that helps in autumn also brings the rot that growers spend the summer fighting.

q: A mild March brings budbreak early, and a clear still night in April drops the temperature below zero. Which hazard is being described?
exp: Green shoots have no defence once they are out, and a single night can remove most of a crop. Frost is the defining risk of the whole valley and the reason for candles, wind machines and sprinklers.

q: A pale red from the Loir valley carries an unmistakable scent of white pepper on a very light frame. Which variety?
exp: Almost extinct a generation ago and now sought after for exactly the peppery lift that once counted against it. It appears in Coteaux du Loir, Coteaux du Vendomois and parts of Touraine.

q: Which variety is the traditional backbone of Anjou's pale, off-dry pink wine?
exp: Grolleau is high-yielding, low in alcohol and pale in colour, which suits a large-volume rose. Cabernet d'Anjou is the separate appellation that uses the Cabernets instead.
